readerTitle: Same sales, opposite futures: what one job tells you
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (가정 청소 서비스, 배달 전문 만두 가게) + 가상 적용 (구독형 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사업 전체의 손익보다 먼저 '한 단위'(한 건, 한 주문, 한 고객)가 돈을 남기는지 본다. 성장은 그 한 단위의 결과를 그대로 곱하기 때문이다.
misconception: 지금 적자여도 규모만 키우면 언젠가 흑자가 된다. 매출이 같으면 두 사업의 건강 상태도 비슷하다.

sources.text: 관리회계와 스타트업 재무의 표준 개념 (단위 경제성, 단위당 매출과 변동비)

factChecks.note: 배달앱 수수료 30%, 앱스토어 수수료 30%는 설명용 가정입니다. 실제 수수료는 플랫폼·국가·요금제에 따라 다르므로(앱스토어는 15%가 적용되는 경우도 있음) 카드에는 가상 사례로만 표시했습니다.
앱 사례: 월 $10 − 스토어 수수료 $3 − AI 처리·서버 비용 $9 = 구독자당 월 −$2. 사용자 수가 늘어도 구독자당 손실은 그대로라는 점만 다룹니다.

cards.title: Same sales, opposite futures: what one job tells you
body: Two small businesses each bring in $30,000 a month. Both are losing money.
One should double its sales as fast as it can. If the other doubles its sales, it loses more. The difference is invisible in the monthly totals.

image.label: A cleaning van and a dumpling takeout bag side by side on a scale
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저울 양쪽에 청소 서비스 밴(작은 모형)과 만두 배달 봉투가 올라가 있고 저울은 정확히 수평. 각각 위에 "$30,000 / month" 라벨. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: You can help one of them grow. Which one?
body: **Home cleaning service:** 300 cleans a month at $100 each. Loses $2,000 a month.
**Delivery-only dumpling kitchen:** 1,500 app orders a month at $20 each. Loses $4,000 a month.
An investor will fund a marketing push to double one business's sales. Which should get it?

options.text: The dumpling kitchen. It has more orders, so growth will spread its rent thinner
options.feedback: Spreading rent helps only if each order leaves money to spread. If each order loses money, more orders mean a bigger loss.

options.text: The cleaning service. Its loss is smaller and closer to fixable
options.feedback: Good pick, though the smaller loss isn't the real reason. The real reason is what each single clean leaves behind. The next two cards show it.

options.text: Neither. Both should cut overhead before growing
options.feedback: Cutting overhead is rarely wrong, but it can't tell you which business growth will save. You'd miss the one that's ready to scale.

cards.title: Follow one clean.
body: Each clean leaves **$40**. The $14,000 a month for the office, scheduling software and insurance is the problem. At 300 cleans, $12,000 doesn't cover it. At 350 cleans, it does.

breakdown.label: Price
breakdown.detail: What the customer pays per clean

breakdown.label: Left per clean
breakdown.detail: Goes toward fixed costs, then profit

cards.title: Follow one dumpling order.
body: Each order **loses $1** before rent is even counted. Busy nights feel like success, but every bag out the door costs the owner a dollar.

cards.title: Unit economics
body: **Unit economics** means looking at the money in and out for one unit of your business: one clean, one order, one customer. The question is simple: does each unit make money or lose it?

Monthly totals mix two things together: costs you pay no matter what, and costs that come with each sale. Looking at one unit pulls them apart. It shows whether a loss is a size problem or a model problem.

image.label: Two magnifying glasses, one over a single clean, one over a single order
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 돋보기 안에 청소 1건 아이콘과 "+$40"(초록), 오른쪽 돋보기 안에 만두 주문 1건 아이콘과 "−$1"(빨강). 돋보기 밖의 큰 숫자 "$30,000"은 흐리게 처리.

cards.title: Growth multiplies whatever one unit does.
body: Double the cleaning service to 600 cleans: 600 × $40 = $24,000, minus $14,000 in fixed costs. It goes from losing $2,000 to making **$10,000** a month.
Double the dumpling kitchen to 3,000 orders: 3,000 × −$1 = −$3,000, minus $2,500 in rent. The loss grows from $4,000 to $5,500.
Same push, opposite result. Growth didn't change either business. It just repeated each unit more times.

cards.title: The unit is whatever you sell, again and again.
body: Choose the thing that repeats and drives your costs:
list: **One job:** a plumber, a cleaner, a moving crew
**One order or cover:** a restaurant, a bakery, a shop
**One customer over time:** a gym, a salon with regulars
**One subscriber per month:** a membership or software plan
cards.callout: Later lessons look at the customer as the unit: what it costs to win one and what one is worth.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the unit is usually one paying account per month. Server, support and payment costs per account can look tiny, until a feature like heavy AI processing makes each active user expensive.

cards.title: One unit can look healthy and still mislead you.
body: Count every cost that really grows with each sale. Leaving out the app commission or the packing hours makes a losing order look fine.
Don't assume the next unit looks like today's. The cleaning service's 500th client may live farther away, so travel costs rise. Cheaper bulk ingredients might help the dumpling kitchen.
And a positive unit isn't a profit yet. Fixed costs still have to be covered by enough units.

cards.title: Now it's a subscription app.
body: A meal-planning app charges $10 a month. The app store keeps 30%, so $3. Its AI recipe feature costs about $9 per subscriber each month to run. The team says: "We're losing money now, but with ten times the users we'll be profitable."
What should they do first?

options.text: Raise money and grow fast. Scale fixes small startups
options.feedback: Each subscriber loses $2 a month, so ten times the users means ten times that loss. Growth would only speed it up.

options.text: Fix one subscriber first: a higher price, a cheaper AI setup, or limits on heavy use
options.feedback: Once each subscriber leaves money, growth starts working for them. It may cost some sign-ups, but those sign-ups were losing money anyway.

options.text: Cut office and salary costs to stretch the runway
options.feedback: That buys time, which helps. But the loss sits in every subscription, so it comes back as soon as the app grows.

cards.title: Before you grow, check that one unit makes money.
body: Growth repeats your unit. If one unit makes money, growth helps. If it loses money, growth makes things worse.
**Try it today:** pick your unit, such as one job, one order or one customer. Write down its price, every cost that comes with it, and what's left.
